title: Davenant: inherent justice not formal cause of strict justification
source_text: XLIV. Quibus consona sunt quae docet Joannes Davenantius Sarisburiensis nuper in Anglia Episcopus, qui de justitia habituali & actuali tractatum edidit accuratissimum. Is enim disputatione de Justitia habituali, cap. 22. sic loquitur, Concedimus esse in omnibus justificatis justitiam quandam inhaerentem, quam si formalem causam statuamus justificationis (liceat enim vocabulum procedere) haud repugnabimus, sed praedictae ju-stificationis, quae respondet stricto examini caelestis judicis, nec formalis, nec meritoria causa ullo modo potest. Tertio vero capite; probat ab hac, infusa, sive inhaerente justitia, fideles, seu renatos omnes vocari & censeri justos; idque ab ipso Deo. Non quidem, quod haec sanctitas infusa, aut inhaerens justitia perfecta sit: sed quod vera, ac minime hypocritica, Deoque nota & grata, qui illam infudit mentibus renatorum. Quod autem saepe apud Reformatos occurrit, per justitiam inhaerentem neminem justum esse coram Deo, cap. 3. docet intelligendum, non quasi simpliciter & absolute dictum, sed comparate solum, & secundum quid. Nempe non aliud significari per hoc, quam nos justitiam nullam habere, qua niti possimus, si stricte discutiamur coram tribunali di-vino: vel nos justitiam non habere quam lex Dei exigit, ad maledicti vitationem, & vitae aeternae consecutionem.
pass_a_gloss: Concordant with which are what John Davenant, lately Bishop of Salisbury in England, teaches, who published a most accurate treatise on habitual and actual righteousness. For in the disputation on Habitual Righteousness, chapter 22, he speaks thus: We concede that there is in all the justified a certain inherent righteousness, which if we establish as the formal cause of justification (for let the word proceed) we will not greatly resist; but of the aforesaid justification which answers to the strict examination of the heavenly Judge it can in no way be either the formal or the meritorious cause. And in the third chapter he proves that from this infused or inherent righteousness all believers or regenerate are called and reckoned just—and that by God himself. Not indeed because this infused holiness or inherent righteousness is perfect, but because it is true and by no means hypocritical, and known and gracious to God who infused it into the minds of the regenerate. But what often occurs among the Reformed—that by inherent righteousness no one is just before God—he teaches in chapter 3 is to be understood not as said simply and absolutely, but only comparatively and in a qualified sense. Namely, that nothing else is signified by this than that we have no righteousness on which we can lean if we are strictly examined before the divine tribunal; or that we do not have the righteousness which God's law requires for avoiding the curse and obtaining eternal life.
pass_b_english: Davenant allows calling inherent justice a formal cause in a loose sense, but not of justification that answers the Judge's strict exam.
Reformed sayings that none is just before God by inherent justice are comparative—not absolute denial of true holiness.
